claims.text: The untreated starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Relatively coarse internal boundaries promote dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces produce local stress concentrations, early microcracking, and catastrophic damage during tensile straining.
Moderate cold rolling followed by subcritical annealing will refine the lamellar spacing without fully recrystallizing or destroying the dual-phase structure.
Cold rolling and subcritical annealing will nucleate hierarchical nanotwins along colony or dual-phase boundaries.
The treatment will produce an ultrafine lamellar microstructure that retains the composite lamellar character.
Refined lamellar spacing provides more spatially distributed barriers and constraints on dislocation motion.
Hierarchical nanotwins provide barriers to dislocation motion and thereby contribute to strengthening.
The refined lamellae and nanotwins disrupt dense dislocation pile-ups at individual lamellar interfaces.
The treated hierarchy will reduce local stress concentrations and delay microcrack initiation.
The treated microstructure will promote more homogeneous plastic flow.
The treatment will significantly increase elongation to failure while maintaining or slightly increasing yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Hierarchical nanotwinning can increase strength without reducing ductility.
The proposed improvement is applicable to eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures.
Excessive rolling or annealing could eliminate beneficial lamellar interfaces or cause unwanted phase transformations, nullifying the strength–ductility synergy.
The claimed benefit should be evaluated by quasi-static tensile testing at room temperature.
Failure to obtain a reproducible statistically significant ductility increase without strength loss, or failure to produce the proposed microstructural changes, would falsify the hypothesis.
